newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S.-Japan treaty covers disputed isles-report.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Japan treaty covers disputed isles-report.

text.p: A U.S. Defence Department official was quoted in a Japanese newspaper on Thursday as saying Japanese-controlled islands disputed by China and Taiwan fall under the terms of the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty.

But the official, Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defence Kurt Campbell, told the Yomiuri Shimbun in an interview that the treaty obligation over the disputed islands did not mean the United States recognised Japan's claims to them.

"The 1972 U.S.-Japan agreement on the return of Okinawa to Japan clarifies that the Senkaku islands fall under Japanese administration. This was clearly specified by the United States for security purposes," Yomiuri quoted Campbell as saying.
The islands in the East China Sea, called Senkakus by Japan and the Diaoyus by China and Taiwan, were controlled by the United States until 1972 when Washington handed back Okinawa to Japan.

Yomiuri said Campbell made it clear that the United States was not taking sides on the islands dispute. Campbell said he was only clarifying the extent of the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty and drew a line between territory effectively administered by Japan and territory that was legally Japan's.
Yomiuri said Campbell's statement meant that the United States was conducting a balancing act between China and Japan.

"The security situation is clear. America made a solemn promise in the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty to defend Japan's territory and areas under its administration in time of emergency. We will keep this promise," Campbell said in the interview.
Campbell also voiced strong U.S. hopes for a peaceful settlement of the dispute.
The dispute flared up in September after the death of a Hong Kong activist in protests near the islands against the construction of a lighthouse on one of the islands by Japanese rightwingers.
In talks in Manila last week, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto tried to cool things down by assuring Chinese President Jiang Zemin that Japan will try to prevent further escalation of the row.
